title: Product Management Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: A product manager owns the 'why' and 'what' — not the 'how' (engineering) or the 'when-to-sell' (sales). The PM sits at the intersection of business viability, technical feasibility, and user desirability; a product must satisfy all three. Jobs-To-Be-Done (JTBD): customers 'hire' a product to make progress in their lives — understand the job, not just the demographic. Outcomes over outputs: shipping features is not success; changing user behavior and business metrics is. The PM has responsibility without authority — influence, not command, is the core skill.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A team ships 12 features and celebrates. Usage is flat. They optimized output (features shipped) instead of outcome (user behavior changed). The right question was never 'what should we build?' but 'what problem are users trying to solve, and did we solve it?'

PRACTICE: 1) Write a JTBD statement for a product you use. 2) Distinguish an output metric from an outcome metric. 3) Identify the desirability/feasibility/viability risk in a product idea.

title: Discovery & Customer Research
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Discovery reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. Qualitative methods (user interviews, observation) reveal *why*; quantitative (analytics, surveys, A/B tests) reveal *what* and *how many*. The Mom Test: never ask 'would you use this?' (people lie to be nice) — ask about past behavior ('tell me about the last time you faced this problem'). Continuous discovery: talk to customers weekly, not once per quarter. Opportunity Solution Trees map the desired outcome → opportunities (pains) → solutions → experiments.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A PM asks 20 users 'would you pay for this?' — 18 say yes. They build it; nobody buys. Reframed via The Mom Test: 'What are you using today, and what did you pay for it?' would have revealed that nobody was spending money on the problem at all. Past behavior predicts; hypothetical enthusiasm doesn't.

PRACTICE: 1) Rewrite three leading questions as behavioral ones. 2) Build an Opportunity Solution Tree. 3) Design one experiment to test a risky assumption.

title: Prioritization & Roadmapping
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Prioritization is the PM's highest-leverage act — saying no is the job. Frameworks: RICE (Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort), MoSCoW (Must/Should/Could/Won't), Kano model (basic needs, performance needs, delighters), Cost of Delay. A roadmap is not a release schedule — it's a communication of themes and outcomes over time, held loosely. Now/Next/Later beats Gantt-style date commitments for uncertain work. Opportunity cost: every 'yes' is an implicit 'no' to everything else.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Two features: A reaches 10,000 users with small impact; B reaches 500 with huge impact. RICE forces explicit scoring rather than gut feel or whoever lobbied hardest. The framework's real value isn't the number — it's making trade-offs visible and defensible to stakeholders.

PRACTICE: 1) Score three features with RICE. 2) Classify features using Kano. 3) Convert a date-based roadmap into Now/Next/Later.

title: Product Strategy & Positioning
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Product strategy answers: who is it for, what problem does it solve, why us, and why now? A product vision is the long-term change you want to create; strategy is the path. Positioning defines the competitive alternative and the unique value you offer against it. The strategy must make trade-offs — a product for everyone is a product for no one. Product-market fit (PMF): when the market pulls the product out of you — measurable by retention, organic growth, and the Sean Ellis test (>40% would be 'very disappointed' without it).

WORKED EXAMPLE: A team measures PMF by signups, which are climbing. But retention at 30 days is 4% — users try it and leave. Signups measured curiosity, not fit. Retention, not acquisition, is the true PMF signal: fit means people come back.

PRACTICE: 1) Write a positioning statement naming the competitive alternative. 2) Define your PMF metric. 3) Identify one trade-off your strategy deliberately makes.

title: Metrics, Experimentation & Analytics
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Choose one North Star Metric that captures the value delivered to users (not vanity). AARRR pirate metrics: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral. Retention is the foundation — without it, acquisition is a leaky bucket. Cohort analysis reveals whether the product is improving over time. A/B testing requires statistical significance (avoid peeking, ensure adequate sample); correlation isn't causation. Beware Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A team optimizes for 'time in app' and adds friction that keeps users hunting for features. Time-in-app rises — the metric improves while the product gets worse. Goodhart's Law in action: the metric was gamed, not the value. A North Star must be a proxy for genuine user value, not engagement for its own sake.

PRACTICE: 1) Define a North Star Metric for a product. 2) Build an AARRR funnel with numbers. 3) Identify a metric that could be gamed and how.

title: Execution, Teams & Stakeholders
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The PM aligns engineering, design, and business without authority — clarity and trust are the currency. Write crisp specs: problem, user, success criteria, constraints, non-goals. Non-goals are as important as goals (they prevent scope creep). Manage up with outcome-focused updates; manage sideways with early involvement, not late approval. Empowered teams (given problems to solve) outperform feature teams (given solutions to build). Handle disagreement with data, user evidence, and shared goals — not authority or volume.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A stakeholder demands a specific feature. Instead of arguing or complying, the PM asks 'what outcome are you trying to achieve?' — revealing the real goal, which a simpler solution addresses better. Reframing from solution to problem defuses politics and produces better products.

PRACTICE: 1) Write a spec with explicit non-goals. 2) Convert a feature demand into a problem statement. 3) Design an outcome-focused stakeholder update.

title: Grandmaster — Platform, Pricing & Growth
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Platform thinking: build capabilities others build on, creating ecosystem leverage and network effects. Pricing is product strategy — value-based pricing (charge a fraction of value created) beats cost-plus. Pricing models: subscription, usage-based, freemium, tiered — each shapes behavior. Growth loops beat funnels: a loop is self-reinforcing (users create content → attracts users). Retention compounds: a 5% retention improvement can outperform doubling acquisition spend. Land-and-expand: enter small, grow within the account.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company spends heavily on acquisition while retention is 60% monthly. They're filling a bucket with a hole — 40% churn means the average customer lasts 2.5 months, so acquisition can never outrun the leak. Fixing retention to 90% (10-month lifespan) quadruples LTV without spending a dollar more on marketing.

PRACTICE: 1) Design a growth loop for a product. 2) Choose a pricing model and justify it. 3) Compute LTV at two retention rates and compare.

title: King Level — Product Leadership & Category Creation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At King level, product leadership becomes company leadership: the product strategy IS the business strategy. Category creation — defining a new market and its language — is the highest form of product work, because the category king captures most of the value. Vision must be specific enough to guide decisions and inspiring enough to attract talent. Portfolio thinking across products: horizon 1 (core), 2 (emerging), 3 (bets). The King-level truth: great products are not the sum of great features — they are the expression of a single, clear point of view about how the world should work, executed with obsessive coherence.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Two companies build similar tools. One adds every requested feature and becomes an incoherent Swiss Army knife. The other refuses 90% of requests to protect a sharp point of view, and becomes the definitive product in its category. Saying no is what makes a product great — coherence beats completeness.

PRACTICE: 1) Articulate a product's point of view in one sentence. 2) Define a category you could create and name it. 3) Map a product portfolio across three horizons.
